title: The Voice of Rome
tagline: The Senate hangs on every word — and words can cut like swords.

scenes.text: Rome, 63 BCE. A conspiracy is unfolding. Lucius Sergius Catilina has plotted to seize the Republic by force. The Senate trembles. The consul — a self-made man who rose from the Italian middle class through nothing but eloquence — prepares to speak.

scenes.speaker: Cicero
scenes.text: How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience? How long will your madness mock us? Do you not see that your plot is known? Quousque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?
The hall falls silent. Catiline rises to defend himself — and finds he cannot. Cicero's words have stripped him bare before Rome. The greatest orator of the ancient world has just saved the Republic.

challenge.instruction: Step into Cicero's sandals: count heads and win over the senators one by one, so the vote to act against Catiline's conspirators carries.
challenge.fact: Cicero's four Catilinarian Orations (63 BCE) are among history's most famous speeches. He secured the Senate's vote to execute the conspirators — and was later exiled for putting Roman citizens to death without trial.

scenes.speaker: Cicero
scenes.text: The law is not merely rules. Law is the bond of civil society, the foundation of liberty, the wellspring of justice. A state without law is merely force wearing a mask.

challenge.instruction: Law, Cicero says, is the bond of the state — and a sound argument leaves an opponent nowhere to go. Find the move that corners him.
challenge.fact: Cicero's Catilinarian Orations cornered the conspirators so completely that even Catiline's allies abandoned him. His rhetoric was his weapon.

scenes.text: Decades later: Caesar is dead. Mark Antony seizes power. And Cicero, old and exhausted, takes up his pen one last time — writing the Philippics against Antony. He knows the cost.

scenes.speaker: Cicero
scenes.text: I know what I risk. Antony will not forget these words. But I have defended this Republic all my life. To be silent now — to be silent now would be to die before my death.

challenge.instruction: Cicero has spoken out against Antony fourteen times, and now a friend sends word in Caesar's old cipher. Turn the wheel to learn whose hand is raised against him.
challenge.fact: After Caesar's assassination, Cicero attacked Mark Antony in the speeches called the Philippics. Antony had him killed in 43 BCE, and his head and hands — which had spoken and written them — were nailed up on the Rostra in the Forum.

challenge.instruction: Cicero loved the wonders of Greek learning, none more than Archimedes' sphere, carried to Rome from Syracuse. Restore its lost wheels so the moon keeps time again.
challenge.fact: More of Cicero's writing survives than of any other Roman: speeches, books of philosophy and rhetoric, and more than 900 letters, many to his friend Atticus. They make him the best-documented person of the ancient world.

challenge.instruction: A republic shows its worth in public works, Cicero wrote — walls, harbours, aqueducts. Route the Aqua Marcia from the Anio springs into Rome.
challenge.fact: The Aqua Marcia entered Rome on arches and carried water up to the Capitol. Two later aqueducts, the Tepula and the Julia, were built on top of its arcades, three channels sharing one line of arches.

scenes.speaker: Cicero
scenes.text: Chanakya and Peseshet hold Rome together, and a follower stands with them. One card alone will not move them. Bring Euclid with me, add both followers, and strike twice.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 2 · Strength in Numbers. Over two turns stack Cicero, Euclid and both followers at Rome, then win two attacks against the rival side.
challenge.fact: An attack compares whole sides at a location, not single cards. Two Great People and two followers in the same stat outweigh a rival who arrived first, and each win sends one rival card back to its owner's hand.
